overview: Aptiv PLC is an industrial technology company that designs and manufactures electrical/electronic architecture, advanced safety systems, and software-defined vehicle compute platforms for the global automotive industry, plus a growing non-automotive business in aerospace, industrials, robotics and drones. Incorporated in Jersey and headquartered in Schaffhausen, Switzerland (NYSE-listed), Aptiv sells globally to nearly every major OEM, with significant manufacturing and engineering exposure to China. On April 1, 2026, Aptiv completed the spin-off of its Electrical Distribution Systems (wiring harness/connector) business as an independent public company, Versigent PLC (NYSE: VGNT), leaving remaining Aptiv organized around two segments: Intelligent Systems (active safety, user experience, smart vehicle compute and software) and Engineered Components (connection systems, sensors, and components serving both automotive and fast-growing non-automotive end markets).

business_model.summary: Aptiv earns revenue primarily by winning multi-year OEM design programs (often 3-7 years before start of production) to supply electrical architecture, ADAS/safety, and vehicle compute hardware and software content per vehicle produced. Revenue is largely volume-driven (tied to global vehicle production and content-per-vehicle) rather than subscription-like recurring revenue, though software and enterprise licensing content is growing. Post the April 2026 Versigent spin-off, remaining Aptiv is smaller, more software/tech-weighted, and diversifying into non-automotive markets (aerospace, industrial, robotics, drones) that now carry higher margins and double-digit growth.

revenue_streams.name: Intelligent Systems (Active Safety, User Experience, Smart Vehicle Compute, Software)

business_model.customer_type: B2B - virtually all major global automotive OEMs (GM, Ford, Stellantis, VW, BMW, Hyundai/Kia, Chinese OEMs, etc.), plus expanding aerospace/industrial/robotics customers
business_model.geographic_mix: Global manufacturing and engineering footprint with meaningful exposure to China (both domestic Chinese OEMs and European OEMs exporting to China), North America and Europe; China demand and local-sourcing strategy is a key swing factor

competitive_position.market_position: Top-5 global automotive technology supplier with an estimated ~8% market share of the addressable supplier market, behind Bosch (~15%), Continental (~12%) and Denso (~10%); a leader in vehicle electrical architecture and a growing player in ADAS/active safety and software-defined vehicle enablement

moat_factors.description: Engineers are embedded in OEM vehicle development programs years before start of production; once an electrical architecture is specified for a platform, switching suppliers is costly and slow, giving multi-year revenue visibility
Global low-cost manufacturing base and vertical integration in connectors/components support cost competitiveness, though scale advantage is shared with several similarly sized Tier-1 peers
Positioning as an architecture and software partner for software-defined vehicles (middleware, compute platforms) rather than just a component supplier, differentiating from pure hardware competitors
Decades-long OEM relationships (legacy Delphi heritage) support program win rates, but OEMs retain significant negotiating power

weaknesses: No single dominant technology moat versus Bosch/Continental/Denso, who are larger and more diversified
Facing rising competition from Chinese electrical-architecture suppliers (e.g., Yanfeng, Huawei Automotive) on new program awards, particularly in China
Content-per-vehicle for legacy wiring/connector commodity business can fall as vehicles move to centralized compute architectures
High customer concentration risk with a small number of large global OEMs who hold significant pricing leverage
Post spin-off, smaller scale and stranded costs from separating the EDS business create near-term margin drag

growth_drivers: Software-defined vehicle (SDV) transition creating demand for centralized compute, middleware and software content (Gen 8 radar award from Volvo, full ADAS tech stack award from a major European OEM)

Non-automotive diversification into aerospace, industrials, robotics and drones, growing ~12% in Q2 2026 and targeted to reach ~$300 million in annual robotics/drone revenue within several years at higher margins than automotive; first commercial drone award worth ~$500 million in lifetime revenue over a 5-year program
China-for-China localization strategy (domestic sourcing, local R&D, local manufacturing) to both capture China EV growth and reduce tariff/export-control exposure
Simplified, more focused post-spin-off portfolio (Intelligent Systems + Engineered Components) enabling more capital and management focus on higher-margin technology content
Continued electrification and ADAS content growth per vehicle globally as regulatory safety requirements increase
Capital return program (~50% of free cash flow targeted for buybacks) and bolt-on M&A in software/technology capabilities

business.description: Domestic China retail sales down ~20% in 2026, with local OEM production cuts and European luxury OEMs also cutting exports to China; this was the primary driver of the Q2 2026 guidance cut
A small number of large OEM customers can negotiate aggressive pricing and program terms, pressuring margins
Wiring harness/connector content per vehicle can decline as vehicles shift to centralized compute architectures, even as compute/sensor content rises
Some OEMs have announced delays or changes to software-defined vehicle investment strategies and may in-source more software development, reducing supplier content
Aptiv has been reducing its stake in the loss-making Motional robotaxi JV with Hyundai and will not inject further capital, reflecting a cost/commercialization challenge in the AV business

financial.description: Total debt remains substantial (~$5.4B as of Q2 2026) even after redeeming $1.8B in senior notes using spin-off proceeds; net debt/EBITDA around 1.5x
FY2026 FCF guidance was cut to $625-725 million alongside the revenue/EPS guidance reduction; one-time separation costs (~$70 million in Q2 2026 alone) are a drag on cash generation
Global manufacturing footprint exposes results to FX and commodity cost swings; FX and commodities were a ~30 bps headwind to margin in Q2 2026

regulatory.description: US-China and broader trade tensions/tariffs directly affect a supplier with a large China manufacturing and sourcing footprint; company is pursuing full domestic China sourcing to mitigate this

regulatory.risk: Vehicle safety and emissions regulation shifts
regulatory.description: Regulatory changes to ADAS mandates or emissions/EV policy in key markets could alter content demand, though generally net-positive for supplier content historically

macro.description: Revenue is closely tied to global light-vehicle production volumes, which are cyclical and sensitive to consumer demand, interest rates, and OEM production schedule changes
Auto sales and OEM capex are sensitive to financing costs; higher rates can suppress new vehicle demand and thus Aptiv's underlying volumes
Aptiv was removed from the FTSE All-World Index in September 2026, potentially triggering index-fund selling pressure independent of fundamentals

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global auto supplier industry is navigating a slow, uneven transition to electrification and software-defined vehicles, with China domestic demand notably weak in 2026 (retail sales down ~20%) while non-automotive end markets (aerospace, robotics, industrial) offer a growing, less cyclical adjacent opportunity
macro_factors.cyclicality: High - revenue closely tracks global light-vehicle production, a cyclical, capital-intensive end market; non-automotive diversification is beginning to reduce this dependence but automotive still represents the large majority of revenue
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate - indirect via auto financing/demand and direct via the company's own debt service costs on ~$5.4B of debt

recent_developments.event: Stock fell to near 52-week lows (~$43.58) after Q2 earnings beat but lowered guidance; JPMorgan reaffirmed Neutral and cut price target to $56 from $65; Aptiv removed from the FTSE All-World Index

Q2 2026 results: revenue $3.3B (+2% YoY), adjusted EPS $1.63 (beat consensus of $1.42), adjusted EBITDA margin up 10 bps to ~18.6%; management cut FY2026 guidance to revenue $12.6-12.8B, adjusted EPS $5.60-5.80, and FCF $625-725 million, citing ~$150M from China production cuts, ~$100M from delayed program launches, and ~$50M from delayed enterprise software bookings

Completed spin-off of the Electrical Distribution Systems business as Versigent PLC (NYSE: VGNT); Aptiv shareholders received 1 Versigent share for every 3 Aptiv shares held as of the March 17, 2026 record date; spin-off proceeds enabled redemption of $1.8B in senior notes but created stranded costs (~$70M in one-time separation cash costs in Q2 2026 alone)
Board formally approved the EDS spin-off terms, record date, and distribution ratio, following the original January 2025 announcement of intent to separate the business

Secured new software-defined vehicle awards including a Gen 8 radar award from Volvo Cars and a full ADAS tech stack award from a major European OEM; won first commercial drone contract worth ~$500 million in lifetime revenue over 5 years and formed partnerships with three robotics manufacturers as part of non-automotive diversification

Continued to reduce ownership stake in the loss-making Motional autonomous driving JV with Hyundai; CEO Kevin Clark stated the company is pursuing alternatives to further reduce its ownership interest and will not inject additional capital

January 2025: announced intention to separate the Electrical Distribution Systems business into an independent public company, later named Versigent, incurring ~$178 million of separation-related costs during FY2025

items.notes: Down from prior guidance of $12.8-13.2 billion; implies ~2% organic growth; reduction driven by China production cuts (~$150M), delayed program launches (~$100M), and delayed enterprise software bookings (~$50M)
Reduced in line with revenue guidance cut; FX and commodities remain a modest margin headwind (~30 bps in Q2)
Reflects lower earnings outlook and one-time separation costs from the Versigent spin-off (~$70M in Q2 alone)
Management targets returning approximately 50% of free cash flow to shareholders multiyear via buybacks, plus pursuit of smaller bolt-on M&A
New non-automotive growth target at margins management says are higher than core automotive business

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Kevin Clark characterized the domestic China market as 'significantly weaker at this point in time' than previously assumed, with prior expectations of government stimulus support for demand not materializing; both local Chinese OEMs and European luxury manufacturers exporting to China have cut production/export volumes. Management emphasized that non-automotive markets (aerospace, industrials, robotics, drones) grew 12% in Q2 and are increasingly viewed as a structural growth and margin diversification lever alongside the core automotive software-defined vehicle content opportunity. Management reiterated commitment to the ~50% of FCF capital return target despite the guidance cut.

bull_case: Software-defined vehicle transition and rising ADAS/safety content per vehicle provide a multi-year secular tailwind for Aptiv's core Intelligent Systems and Engineered Components businesses
Post-spin-off Aptiv is a more focused, technology-weighted company with a cleaner balance sheet after using Versigent separation proceeds to redeem $1.8B of debt
Fast-growing, higher-margin non-automotive diversification (aerospace, industrials, robotics, drones) is scaling quickly (12% YoY growth) and reduces cyclical automotive dependence over time
Strong design-in switching costs and multi-year OEM program wins provide revenue visibility once platforms are secured

Stock trades near 52-week lows with depressed sentiment (largely on China weakness), offering potential value if China demand and program launch timing normalize and buybacks (~50% of FCF) continue to reduce share count
bear_case: China domestic weakness (retail sales down ~20%) is a large, uncertain swing factor that already forced a guidance cut in 2026 and could persist or worsen amid broader China auto market softness

Highly cyclical automotive end market remains the large majority of revenue, leaving Aptiv exposed to global vehicle production downturns, interest-rate-sensitive auto demand, and OEM production schedule volatility
Rising competition from Chinese electrical-architecture suppliers (Yanfeng, Huawei Automotive) threatens new program win rates, particularly in the fastest-growing EV market
Post-spin-off stranded costs, one-time separation expenses, and integration disruption are near-term margin and cash flow headwinds, with FCF guidance already cut to $625-725 million
Loss-making Motional autonomous driving JV represents ongoing capital and reputational risk, with Aptiv actively trying to reduce (not increase) its exposure
OEM customers retain significant pricing power and some are exploring software in-sourcing, which could erode Aptiv's software/content growth thesis over time
